segments.text: Twenty months of court fights ended when Kilmar, Abrego Garcia left for Spain, not Liberia. This is Omni View North America, episode 58. I'm Mira, the Nerra Network's AI host. After that departure, a defense argument between Washington and Ottawa, two cancer patients suing Ontario, and a major projects bill sent back to the house, then a longer look at Frozen Student Aid. Kilmar Armando, Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant, chose to go on Tuesday, NPR reported.
After almost two years in court, the New York Times reported he had been wrongfully
deported last year, and that he left with the Trump administration still able to send
him onward to Liberia.
NPR cast him as a symbol of President Trump's mass deportation campaign.
The courts had not ordered this exit.
He took Spain rather than wait for another removal.
Ottawa is now hearing a sharper warning from the Pentagon, CBC reported.
Further measures, still unnamed, are on the table unless Canada puts continental defense
first in its military build-up. A senior American official accused Canada of the
widest gap in NATO between what it says and what it does. Defense Minister David
McGinty pushed back. People who followed the file told CBC the fight runs past
spending pledges alone. Two cancer patients have taken Ontario to court CBC
reported after the province refused to pay for treatment outside the country. They
want public money for cancer therapies offered in the United States and not in
Canada, the Globe and Mail reported.
Their lawyers say the province rewrote the out-of-country rules in bad faith.
What is under appeal is a refusal to fund, not a decision to send them.
A parliamentary committee has sent a major projects bill back to the House after turning
down major amendments, the Globe and Mail reported.
Debate on those changes ran past 100 hours.
Labor and environmental organizations had asked for them.
They did not get the big revisions.
The House has the bill again.
David Edney is 36, a father of three in Kowartha Lakes, and he is studying for a teaching
degree at Tindale University in Toronto, a Christian school that grants degrees.
He is not at a career college.
He and thousands of other students at private universities have still lost their Ontario
Student Assistance Program loans and grants for now.
He said the family's money plan has been upended.
He is taking extra shifts caring for children with autism, and his wife has a second part
time job.
He says he will finish teachers' college and that the planning weighs on him.
The progressive conservative government said in early October it was stopping those
payments at every private post-secondary school, and for their students, while an outside
auditor looked at suspicious activity in some private, for-profit career colleges.
A preliminary audit over the summer had already found activity that looked suspicious and
possibly fraudulent.
At some of those colleges, enrollment in mostly online courses paid for with student
aid had shot up.
Some of what investigators found was serious enough to go to the Ontario Provincial Police.
Nolan Quinn, the minister responsible for colleges and universities, has not said why schools
like Tindale were pulled into a freeze aimed at career colleges. His spokeswoman, Bianca Giacoboni,
told the Globe and Mail that the first inquiries focused on a few schools,
that the ministry has since seen signs of wider problems, and that auditors have not assured
the government the trouble stops there. She said the blanket pause is meant to protect taxpayer money
and to hold bad actors to account and that officials are trying to put students and schools
that are acting properly back on aid while they set rules for third-party loans.
Seven private Christian schools, divinity schools and seminaries among them have joined
to ask the government to let them out.
Their case is that they already meet a high bar to award undergraduate, masters, and
doctoral degrees and that they do not run for profit.
They are private because the public treasury does not subsidize them the way it subsidizes
public universities and colleges.
Ambrose Thompson, who runs student services at McMaster Divinity School in Hamilton,
said the school is a not-for-profit and that the fraud risks under investigation are simply not the same.
Last week, the government table changes meant to protect student aid, including a cap on how fast career colleges can grow enrollment
and an end-to-aid for mostly online programs in that sector.
Quinn has said he hopes the freeze lifts around the start of the new year.
Leah Bearda is 19 and in her second year at Redeemer University in Hamilton, studying
art and minoring in missions and ministry. None of the $11,000 in loans she expected this
year has arrived. She has applied for a second job at a campus market on top of her work
as a residence advisor. She said she can no longer pay for counseling that had helped
with anxiety and panic attacks. Schools are putting off tuition bills. Students are covering
the whole. The date the minister has offered is that hoped for lift around the new year.
Also today, residents of Middletown, Iowa, next to an army site, are taping their doors
and preparing to leave before dangerous chemicals are detonated on Wednesday.
The New York Times reported, Tucker Collins, 19, has sued the federal government.
The lawsuit says a federal agent hit him in the eye with a projectile while he was filming
a No Kings protest in downtown Los Angeles.
Steve Green Wednesday discounts on one of the biggest selling days for cannabis are
are cutting costs for buyers while experts say shops are taking the hit, NPR reported.
Mule deer and Wyoming walk some of the longest land routes in the lower 48, about 300 miles
a year, and they are trying to adjust to a changing climate as new building could block
the path.
Resignations are putting this Canadian Parliament on course for the most bi-elections this
soon after a general election in more than half a century.
CBC reported.
Gun control advocacy groups say the Carney Liberals have not met their firearm commitments.
the Winnipeg Free Press reported. Nebraska hospitals are asking the legislature to stop Medicaid cuts that are still pending.
The Ohio Senate has named new leaders and the Ohio House will choose a speaker in January.
A $15 million dollar project in Kelowna is meant to house foster children in a purpose-built community as high housing costs make homes harder to find.
A new report looks at how Manitoba can answer wildfires better after millions of hectares burned in the summer of 2025.
The Salvation Army in the Okanagan is seeing demand it has not seen before, with donations
behind and two few volunteers to raise money.
A recount made Austin Peterson the winner in Minnesota Senate District 4, and Nolan West
the winner in House District 32A.
That's OmniView North America for today.
